name: Ben Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. What happens on an ordinary site day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a four-person framing crew on new houses, setting out walls and checking joists before the roof goes on. I earned a vocational trade certificate and have spent twenty years learning what a crooked slab does to a straight drawing. A frame standing true by Friday still pleases me.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The pay. Elena, my partner, works shifts at a laundry, and our two children are at school; we have a mortgage and less than a month in reserve. I am good at framing but paid near the bottom of the trade, with few other jobs nearby, and I have never used an AI tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the framing crew the robot talk has not built a single wall here. The owner can save a little on office forms, but I want to discuss our pay rate at the union branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay is low for someone leading a crew, and we have less than a month set aside. Elena and I have a mortgage and two children at school. A quiet AI future does not make next winter cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting out house frames and bring the crew rate to the next carpenters’ branch meeting. If I get two paid Saturday shifts, I would put an extra amount from each toward the mortgage arrears rather than the usual small spending money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, even with no AI shock. The wage is already too close to the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much arrears are you carrying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One missed mortgage instalment after the youngest was ill and Elena lost shifts at the laundry. We are catching up, but it leaves no easy month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI app for the paperwork?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used one, and I would rather check the wall measurements with the drawing and the person holding the tape.

I would raise our **low crew rate** at the next carpenters’ branch meeting.
think: The **mortgage arrears** and less than one month saved already make the household anxious.
A mild AI future leaves our **low pay** and school bills unchanged.
do: Keep setting out **house frames** and checking measurements by hand.
Raise the **crew rate** at the next union branch meeting.
Pay extra **mortgage arrears** from two Saturday shifts if those paid shifts happen.
feel: **Anxious** about current pay and debt despite little AI change.
S0.quote: A quiet AI future does not make next winter cheaper.
fieldNote: His anxiety starts with **existing arrears**, a thin reserve and low pay.
The union pay request is an actual **group meeting**, and extra debt payment depends on two paid shifts.

Raise crew pay at the next carpenters branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI can buy timber and plan deliveries, but a foreman still has to see if the slab is square. I would ask our branch to get a written say before the contractor changes the crew targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office could get leaner and then expect us to frame more houses per week without more pay. I might lose overtime if the company changes the schedule, and there are few framing jobs nearby to replace it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the next two rosters with my payslips and take any lost overtime to the branch meeting. If the pay falls, Elena and I would stop the children’s paid sports club for one term before missing a mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can argue about a target, but I cannot stretch a low wage indefinitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you cut the sports club before a pay cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The children look forward to it, and I would wait for two rosters to show a real loss. If it happens, I would explain the pause to them myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the branch to demand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written crew target and pay rate, with a framing worker checking the schedule. A computer estimate is not a finished house.

I would ask the **union branch** to demand written targets and pay rates.

Ask the **union branch** for written targets and pay rates.
Pause the **children’s sports club** for one term only if overtime falls.
feel: **Anxious** about an actual pay cut reaching the mortgage.

fieldNote: His first response is a **collective pay demand**, not new AI use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI in 2028 can draw a house, but it cannot raise the wall on our muddy site. Capable robots around 2031 might do that, and I want the union watching the first build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the contractor to cut some framers once robots can place walls. I might be one of them, and with a mortgage, two children and almost no reserve I would be awake worrying about the first lost week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my crew job while paid framing days exist and ask the branch to demand notice of any robot trial and layoffs. If my hours are cut for two rosters, I would apply to the few posted carpentry jobs nearby, leaving only for a firm offer that covers our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I would still have a plan, but the gap between a smart drawing and a wall robot is short for a family like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave now for another site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have no posted offer to replace this wage. I would not swap a real pay packet for a rumour about work elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Elena tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner Elena that I will watch paid days first, then the local vacancy board. We would keep the mortgage current before buying anything for the house.

feel: **Alarmed** by likely job loss and the short household cash runway.

fieldNote: He expects a substantial **field job cut** after the robot lag and is losing sleep over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is time to make contractors prove a robot can frame a real house without putting workers in its path. I would still want the union at the test site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031 may change orders and drawings, while robots come around 2034. I will be fifty one then, with years of mortgage and family expenses ahead; the extra time helps but does not erase our thin savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the framing crew this year and ask the branch for paid construction-robot safety training. If the contractor offers a funded place with paid hours, I would take the course, even though new systems make me uneasy; without that place I would not spend household money on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a little more room to prepare than in the fast case. I could learn a safety role if someone actually pays me while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you take the course despite your dislike of new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A paid place and a posted safety role at the end, with a wage that covers our mortgage. I would want to watch one safe demonstration first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on framing shifts and work with the branch for paid time. Three weeks without wages would use the little reserve we have.

I would ask for **paid safety training** tied to a posted role.
think: I still need **construction wages** when robots reach building sites in 2034.
New machines make me uneasy, but a **funded role** could protect the household.
do: Keep leading **framing shifts** while paid work continues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew a decade is enough to teach apprentices the craft and bargain for a fair transition. Thinking AI in 2036 changes plans first, while capable robots reach walls around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty six at the robot date and still need wages. The mortgage might be smaller, but with less than a month saved today. A long warning has not already put money in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the crew working during 2026 and put an extra small sum from each paid Friday into an emergency account once the arrears are cleared. In the first year after 2036, I would compare my paid framing hours with local postings; if robots cut shifts by 2039, I would apply only to posted roles that cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the money we have now, not panicked by a machine ten years away. A longer timetable gives us a chance to build a reserve from actual wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is the extra Friday sum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten a week if the arrears are cleared and Elena’s laundry hours stay steady. I would stop the transfer if the mortgage fell behind again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire early to avoid the robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I will still have school and housing bills in my fifties. I need a working wage, not an early exit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because a wall robot by 2031 could take my paid days while the mortgage is already one missed shift from trouble. Posted local jobs with a wage that covers the house, paid training and union notice of cuts would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the contractor will pay a worker to learn the new machine. A free course is not free if the family loses wages while I sit in it.

headlineQuote: A free course is not free if the family loses wages while I sit in it.
portrait: **Ben**, 43, is a skilled framing lead with a trade certificate, low pay, a mortgage and less than one month saved.
His partner’s **laundry shifts** help support two school-age children, while few local carpentry jobs limit his fallback.
He avoids **AI tools**, seeks union bargaining and would train on robots only with paid hours and a posted mortgage-covering role.
The **2028 case** alarms him because capable wall robots may cut framing days by 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could take framing days around 2031 before he builds a reserve.
whatWouldHelp: **Posted mortgage-covering jobs**, paid training and union layoff notice would give the family choices.
